principle: Everything that follows from state being a binding record, not a desired-state source of truth
because: T-002 establishes that state's only job is binding already-created objects to configuration and refreshing before any operation; T-006 shows plan literally performing that refresh-then-diff first; T-001 and T-008 only work because centralizing or read-only-sharing a binding record is safe in a way sharing a 'desired state' would not be; and T-035's incident is exactly what happens when a team assumes state itself is what apply converges toward instead of configuration.

principle: Locking guards against concurrent writers, not against a human confirming the wrong command
because: Locking (T-004) and its concrete backend implementation (T-046) exist to stop two processes writing state at once, not to stop a single confirmed destructive command; force-unlock (T-005) is the manual override for the first case, and T-029/T-048 show how that override becomes its own hazard once a human second-guesses it by hand; T-034 is the case where the team assumed Terraform's own protections would catch a wrong-context destroy and learned the protection that saved them lived in Azure, not Terraform.

principle: Parallel execution is safe only because graph construction already resolved dependencies and cycles first
because: The 9-phase construction in T-027 adds nodes, wires depends_on and interpolation edges, and validates a single acyclic root before any walk begins; T-028's depth-first-with-parallelism traversal and its default concurrency of 10 are only correct because that validation already happened - the concurrency knob is safe to turn precisely because it operates on a graph whose ordering constraints were proven, not assumed.

principle: Two competing disciplines for closing the time gap between a plan being computed and being applied
because: T-007 and T-036 give what look like the same advice but aren't: T-007 says re-check the final plan right before applying because a speculative plan can go stale, while T-036 says save a plan to a file and apply that file exactly, without re-planning at all - two different answers to the same time-gap problem, in real tension with each other; T-040 is what happens when neither discipline is enough, because the provider itself can reject at apply time what planning correctly predicted a moment before.

principle: The same portability that lets a CI plan file cross machines is what exposes it in cleartext
because: T-020's requirement that plan and apply run as separate CI steps sharing one archived working directory is what forces the plan to persist to disk between stages at all; T-021 shows credentials can be kept off disk via env vars, but T-056 shows the plan file itself cannot be - HashiCorp states outright that any sensitive data in a plan is saved in cleartext, so the same split that makes review and portability possible is what turns the artifact into a wider-audience leak.

principle: Two independent gates inserted at the same seam between plan and apply, one human and one machine
because: T-022's VCS-triggered speculative plan and T-026's policy-as-code evaluation are structurally the same move performed by different actors: both intercept a run at the identical seam between plan and apply rather than changing what plan or apply compute, one requiring a human reviewer to read the diff and the other requiring an automated policy set to pass before the run is allowed to continue.

principle: Standing access versus run-scoped access, applied at every layer of CI/CD credentialing
because: T-019's seven-step OIDC exchange, T-041's case for preferring it over static keys, and T-050's drill converting a pipeline from one to the other are all instances of a single tradeoff that T-044's stored-token tutorial sits on the opposite side of and T-045's tutorial sits on the OIDC side of: whether the CI/CD pipeline holds a standing secret that exists independent of any run, or a credential scoped to and torn down with the run that requested it.

principle: Environment identity is never self-verifying, whether it's a workspace selector or a copied backend key
because: T-009 and T-010 establish that CLI workspaces share one backend and one set of credentials with no directory-level signal of which is selected; T-003 is the mechanism (partial backend configuration) that lets directories avoid that by giving each environment its own backend config; T-030 and T-032 are incidents on each side of that same failure mode - an invisible workspace selector and a copied backend key that was never updated - showing directories are the recommended fix (T-031) but not an automatic one; T-051 drills both failure modes side by side.

principle: Splitting scope to shrink blast radius, the same design move drawn at the account layer and the state layer
because: T-023's account-per-environment split and T-033's state-file-per-service-and-lifecycle split are the same design decision made at two different layers - one drawn in cloud IAM boundaries, the other in Terraform's own state boundaries - and T-033's near-miss shows what happens when only the state-layer boundary is missing: a single operation's blast radius covers everything in one shared file regardless of how carefully accounts were separated.

principle: A module built as a stable interface for a consumer who never opens its internals
because: Dependency inversion (T-012) and preconditions (T-013) exist so a module's consumer never has to open its internals to know what it needs or assumes; flat trees and shallow nesting (T-011, T-016) keep that contract traceable instead of buried in a chain; scoping by encapsulation, privilege, and volatility (T-015) draws the boundary so the interface doesn't leak scope it shouldn't; data-only modules (T-014) and shipping underspecified-but-over-exposed (T-017) are the same idea applied to reads and outputs; T-042 and T-049 are what building and then deliberately breaking that contract look like in practice.

principle: The lock file's reproducibility guarantee stops at the provider boundary and never reaches modules
because: T-053 establishes that a committed lock file makes provider version resolution durable and identical across every machine that runs init; T-054 shows that same guarantee was never extended to modules - Terraform will always resolve the newest module version matching a constraint, with no lock file involvement at all - so a team that trusts the committed lock file to have frozen 'the dependency set' has left one entire class of dependency unpinned without knowing it.

principle: Terraform infers resource identity from address or index, never from intent
because: T-037's count-based collections track resources by list position, so removing one element shifts every later index and makes Terraform touch resources nobody changed; T-038's address-based tracking treats a rename as delete-and-recreate unless a moved block says otherwise - different mechanisms, but the same underlying fact: Terraform never infers 'this is still the same resource' from context, only from an explicit key, and both traps are what happens when a team assumes it does.

principle: Drift is invisible until something runs a plan, automated or not
because: T-039 establishes there is no ambient detection loop - Terraform only sees drift the moment something runs a plan; T-024's HCP health assessments are that same manual mechanism (refresh-only plans) running on a schedule rather than continuously, which is exactly why T-025's distinction holds: they catch configuration drift but not state drift, because both are still just a plan being run against real infrastructure; T-043 and T-052 are the same -refresh-only-and-import sequence demonstrated by hand, whether or not HCP is doing the scheduling.

principle: Secrets land in cleartext on disk regardless of the sensitive flag, in state and in saved plans alike
because: T-055 establishes that state stores real values in plaintext regardless of how they got there, and that marking a variable sensitive only hides it from terminal output while backend-specific encryption is what actually protects the file at rest; T-047's certification questions test the same fact directly (secrets referenced as variables end up in plaintext in state) - the 'sensitive' flag and backend encryption solve two different halves of the same leak, and testing on one doesn't confirm the other is in place.
